intro.data: Every order arrives as EITHER a card charge OR a cash drop, and BOTH must end as the same kind of slip: a total paired with its tax. First case-split the order to a raw amount, then pair that amount with its tax. The tray hides look-alikes: a handler that gets the card right but mishandles the cash, a bundler that swaps total and tax, and a bundler that fakes the tax. Wire the ONE chain that nails the card order AND the cash order.
intro.alchemy: Every draught arrives as EITHER an acid pour OR a base pour, and BOTH must end as the same vial: a measure paired with its residue. First case-split the draught to a raw measure, then pair that measure with its residue. The tray hides look-alikes: a handler right on acid but wrong on base, a binder that swaps measure and residue, and a binder that fakes the residue. Wire the ONE chain that settles the acid AND the base.
intro.spellcraft: Every casting arrives as EITHER a ward sign OR a hex sign, and BOTH must end as the same sigil: a charge paired with its echo. First case-split the casting to a raw charge, then pair that charge with its echo. The tray hides look-alikes: a working right on the ward but wrong on the hex, a weaver that swaps charge and echo, and a weaver that fakes the echo. Wire the ONE chain that binds the ward AND the hex.
intro.abstract: ι₁ a tags a as the left option and ι₂ b the right; [f,g] : A+B → Y runs the matching branch; (m,n) is the pair holding m then n, and the pairing ⟨p,q⟩ : Y → M×N builds (y, 2y). One chain A+B → Y → M×N must pass two cases: ι₁ 3 ↦ (5,10) and ι₂ 4 ↦ (8,16). The case-split impostor [f,g′]? matches [f,g] on ι₁ but sends ι₂ 4 ↦ 9 (should be 8), so it passes case 1 and fails case 2; the swapped pairing ⟨q,p⟩ and the faking pairing ⟨p,q⟩? are wrong. Wire [f,g] then ⟨p,q⟩ and leave the rest in the tray.

goal.data: Bring the case-split handler, the raw-amount table, and the right bundler, and wire ONE chain that turns the card order into (total 5, tax 10) AND the cash order into (total 8, tax 16).
goal.alchemy: Bring the case-split handler, the raw-measure vessel, and the right binder, and wire ONE chain that turns the acid pour into (measure 5, residue 10) AND the base pour into (measure 8, residue 16).
goal.spellcraft: Bring the case-split working, the raw-charge flame, and the right weaver, and wire ONE chain that turns the ward sign into (charge 5, echo 10) AND the hex sign into (charge 8, echo 16).
goal.abstract: Place Y and wire one A+B → Y → M×N chain ([f,g] then ⟨p,q⟩) that sends ι₁ 3 ↦ (5,10) and ι₂ 4 ↦ (8,16).

description.alchemy: a vial bundling a measure and its residue
description.spellcraft: a sigil bundling a charge and its echo

description.alchemy: one handler that reads the raw measure from BOTH pours — acid AND base

description.alchemy: pairs the measure with its residue (double) — measure first, residue second

afterSuccess.data: One chain handled both orders: Take Amount read the raw amount from the card AND the cash, then Bundle Slip paired each amount with its tax — card ↦ (5,10) and cash ↦ (8,16). The handler that mishandled the cash matched the good one on the card but drifted on the cash, so it passed the easy case and failed the hard one; the swapping and faking bundlers broke the pair. A pipeline is a coproduct case-split feeding a product pairing: ⟨p,q⟩ ∘ [f,g].
afterSuccess.alchemy: One chain settled both pours: Take Measure read both acid and base, then Bind Vial paired each measure with its residue — acid ↦ (5,10) and base ↦ (8,16). The handler that mishandled the base matched on the acid but drifted on the base; the swapping and faking binders broke the pair. The pipeline is ⟨p,q⟩ ∘ [f,g].
afterSuccess.spellcraft: One chain bound both signs: Take Charge read both ward and hex, then Weave Sigil paired each charge with its echo — ward ↦ (5,10) and hex ↦ (8,16). The working that mishandled the hex matched on the ward but drifted on the hex; the swapping and faking weavers broke the pair. The pipeline is ⟨p,q⟩ ∘ [f,g].
afterSuccess.abstract: The faithful composite ⟨p,q⟩ ∘ [f,g] sent ι₁ 3 ↦ (5,10) and ι₂ 4 ↦ (8,16). [f,g′]? agrees with [f,g] on ι₁ (both give 5) so case 1 passes, but on ι₂ it gives 9 not 8, so the pairing lands on (9,18) and case 2 fails. The swapped ⟨q,p⟩ reverses the components and ⟨p,q⟩? fakes the second — two cases pin both the OR-branch and the AND-bundle.

reveal.summary: A real pipeline can combine a coproduct and a product: case-split the input with [f,g] : A+B → Y, then pair the result with ⟨p,q⟩ : Y → M×N. Two cases (one per injection) force every branch of the OR and every component of the AND to be correct: ⟨p,q⟩ ∘ [f,g] must send ι₁ 3 ↦ (5,10) AND ι₂ 4 ↦ (8,16).
reveal.moreFormal: [f,g] is the unique map out of the coproduct with [f,g]∘ι₁ = f and [f,g]∘ι₂ = g; ⟨p,q⟩ is the unique map into the product with π₁∘⟨p,q⟩ = p and π₂∘⟨p,q⟩ = q. Composing them threads 'or' into 'and'.
reveal.programmerAnalogy: const run = (o: Card | Cash) => { const y = match(o){...}; return [y, 2*y] as const }; one bad branch or one wrong tuple slot and a second case catches it.
